title: Designing S3-like Object Storage: Metadata, Data Placement, and Erasure Coding
lesson:
An object store holds immutable blobs addressed by bucket and key, and is built for durability and scale rather than low latency or in-place edits. Its architecture separates a metadata service, which maps bucket and key to the object's version, size, and the locations of its data, from a data store that holds the bytes. A stateless API layer authenticates requests, consults the metadata service, and streams data to and from data nodes. Keeping the two planes separate lets each scale independently: metadata is many small records, data is few large ones.

Large objects are split into chunks or parts, which allows parallel multipart upload, resumable uploads, and spreading one object across many nodes. A placement service picks the nodes for each chunk, usually across failure domains such as racks and zones. Because objects are immutable, an update writes a new version and the metadata pointer is switched afterwards, so readers see either the old or the new object, never a torn one. Deletes mark the metadata, and garbage collection reclaims orphaned chunks later.

Durability comes from redundancy. Three-way replication is simple and fast to read but costs 3x the storage. Erasure coding splits data into k data fragments plus m parity fragments, and any k of the k+m fragments can rebuild the object; for example 8 data plus 4 parity tolerates losing any 4 fragments at 1.5x storage overhead. The trade-offs are more CPU and slower reconstruction, and reads that touch many nodes, so erasure coding is common for large, colder objects while small or hot objects may be replicated.

Background processes maintain the guarantees: checksums are verified on read and by periodic scrubbing to detect silent corruption, and lost fragments are rebuilt on healthy nodes when a disk or node fails. Metadata is typically stored in a replicated, sharded database, since losing it makes the data unreachable even if the bytes are intact.

questions.prompt: Why do object stores separate the metadata service from the data store?
options: Because metadata (many small records) and data (few large blobs) have different scaling needs
To make objects mutable in place
questions.explanation: Each plane has a different access pattern and size profile, so splitting them allows independent scaling.

questions.prompt: With erasure coding of 8 data fragments plus 4 parity fragments, how many fragments can be lost while still recovering the object?
questions.explanation: Any 8 of the 12 fragments suffice to reconstruct the data, so up to 4 can be lost.

questions.prompt: Three-way replication has a storage overhead of 3x, whereas 8+4 erasure coding has an overhead of ____x.
questions.explanation: 12 total fragments for 8 fragments' worth of data is 12/8 = 1.5x.

questions.prompt: Because stored objects are immutable, updating one is done by writing a new version and then switching the metadata pointer.
questions.explanation: Readers see either the old or the new version, never a partially written object.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a multipart object upload.
items: Commit the metadata entry pointing to the parts
Upload parts in parallel to chosen data nodes
Placement service selects nodes across failure domains
questions.explanation: Parts are made, nodes are chosen, parts are uploaded, and only then is the object made visible through metadata.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of periodic scrubbing in an object store?
options: Detecting silent data corruption by verifying checksums so damaged fragments can be repaired
questions.explanation: Scrubbing finds bit rot before it accumulates beyond what redundancy can repair.
